parts.partTitle: Why Naive Caching Fails at Scale

beats.headline: Why does your cache crash your database?
beats.subline: When a hot key expires, your pods trigger a stampede.
beats.narration: Your cache is supposed to protect PostgreSQL, but under high load, it often becomes the exact mechanism that knocks it over. Let's look at why naive caching breaks.

beats.title: The Cache Stampede
beats.subtitle: Multiple pods hitting the DB simultaneously
beats.narration: When a hot key expires, every pod sees a miss at the same millisecond. They all fire identical heavy queries to PostgreSQL, exhausting your connection pool and triggering a latency cascade.

beats.title: Cache-Aside vs Write-Through

top.label: Cache-Aside (Default)
points: Evict on write to avoid stale data

beats.narration: Cache-Aside is standard for Java services. Always delete the cache key on writes rather than updating it, to avoid ordering races where stale data overwrites fresh state.

beats.title: Defending Against Penetration

steps.explanation: Prevents attackers from hammering the DB with non-existent IDs.

beats.narration: Use a null sentinel to cache negative lookups. This stops cache penetration, where attackers request random IDs that don't exist, forcing every request to hit your database.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
takeaways: Use null sentinels for negative lookups
Avoid fixed TTLs to prevent avalanches
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 2): Why JVM locks fail in Kubernetes →
beats.narration: That's the foundation. In Part 2, we see why your synchronized blocks fail across multiple pods and how to build a real distributed lock.

beats.headline: Why synchronized blocks are useless in Kubernetes.
beats.subline: JVM locks only see their own heap. You need a shared state.
beats.narration: Synchronized blocks only guard threads inside a single JVM. If you run ten Kubernetes pods, you have ten independent locks. You need a distributed lock in Redis.

beats.title: The Redisson Watchdog

steps.explanation: Redisson extends the TTL automatically if the pod is still alive.

beats.narration: Redisson is the industry standard. Its Watchdog timer periodically extends the lock's TTL via Lua scripts, ensuring the lock doesn't expire while your thread is still processing.

beats.title: The Watchdog Mechanism
beats.subtitle: Preventing premature expiration
beats.narration: The Watchdog runs on a Netty timer thread. If your pod crashes, the timer dies, and Redis expires the lock. No deadlocks, no manual cleanup.

beats.title: Atomic Lua Deletion
beats.caption: Never delete another pod's lock

lines.text: Lua script ensures only the owner can delete

beats.narration: Never use a simple DEL command. If a GC pause causes your lock to expire, you might accidentally delete a lock just acquired by another pod. Always use Lua to verify ownership.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In
takeaways: Always use Lua for atomic release
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 3): The GC pause trap →
beats.narration: Locks are great, but they aren't magic. In Part 3, we see why even Redisson can't save you from a 40-second stop-the-world GC pause.

beats.headline: Your lock is lying to you.
beats.subline: A long GC pause can invalidate your distributed lock.
beats.narration: A 40-second stop-the-world GC pause freezes your app. The Watchdog can't renew the lock, Redis expires it, and another pod takes over. Your app resumes and corrupts the data.

beats.title: The GC Pause Corruption
beats.subtitle: Why locks aren't enough for state
beats.narration: Pod 2 thinks it has exclusive access. Pod 1 wakes up, unaware it lost the lock, and writes to the database. You have a race condition, even with a lock.

beats.title: Fencing Tokens to the Rescue
beats.code:
UPDATE inventory_reservations
SET qty = qty + :qty,
    fencing_token = :token
WHERE sku = :sku
  AND fencing_token < :token;

steps.explanation: The DB rejects any request with an older token than the one it already processed.

beats.narration: The solution is a fencing token. Every time you acquire a lock, the service increments a counter. The database only accepts writes if the token is higher than the last one.

beats.title: Efficiency vs Correctness

bottom.label: Correctness Locking
bottom.code:
UPDATE ... WHERE version = :v
// Or etcd + fencing

beats.narration: Use Redis locks for efficiency, like preventing cache stampedes. Use database-level optimistic locking or consensus-backed tokens for correctness, like financial transactions.

beats.title: Part 3 Locked In
beats.narration: You now know the difference between efficiency and correctness. In Part 4, we use Bloom filters to stop cache penetration attacks.

beats.headline: Stop hitting your DB for fake IDs.
beats.subline: Bloom filters can reject invalid requests in memory.
beats.narration: Attackers love requesting non-existent IDs to force DB lookups. Don't waste your database CPU. Use a Bloom filter to reject these requests instantly.

beats.title: Bloom Filter Logic
beats.subtitle: Probabilistic membership test
beats.narration: A Bloom filter is a compact bit array. If it says 'no', the ID definitely doesn't exist. If it says 'yes', it probably exists. It's a perfect shield for your database.

beats.title: Redisson Bloom Filter

steps.explanation: Reject invalid IDs before hitting Redis or PostgreSQL.

beats.narration: Initialize the filter with expected size and error rate. If the filter returns false, you save a network call to Redis and a query to PostgreSQL. It's incredibly fast.

beats.title: Bloom Filter Trade-offs
beats.caption: Operational constraints
beats.narration: Remember, Bloom filters can't delete items. You'll need to rebuild them periodically or use Cuckoo filters if your dataset changes frequently. Always plan for the cold start.

beats.title: Part 4 Locked In
beats.narration: You're now ready to build production-grade caches. In Part 5, we wrap up with the ultimate caching checklist.

beats.headline: Don't build your own locking logic.
beats.narration: Distributed locking is deceptively simple but architecturally dangerous. Don't roll your own. Use Redisson, respect the Watchdog, and always use fencing tokens for correctness.

beats.title: The Caching Checklist

top.label: The Good

bottom.label: The Bad

beats.narration: Follow this checklist. Avoid fixed TTLs, never rely on JVM locks for cluster coordination, and always validate your storage layer with fencing tokens if you care about data integrity.
